properties.name: Amber Road
properties.notes: Pliny the Elder records a Roman knight sent north under Nero to buy amber directly at the source, a round trip of some 600 Roman miles from Carnuntum that returned with enough amber to decorate the netting, weapons, and biers used in a single day of gladiatorial games. From Carnuntum south to Aquileia the route followed the empire's own paved road network through Scarbantia, Savaria, Sala, Poetovio, Celeia, and Emona, not through Vindobona, which lay upstream on a separate Danube road. North of Carnuntum the road crossed unannexed Germania to the Baltic amber coast; no continuous ancient road bed survives there, so this stretch is drawn as a reasonable line between attested anchor points rather than a mapped road.
sources: Itin. Ant.; Tabula Peutingeriana (Aquileia-Emona-Celeia-Poetovio-Sala-Savaria-Scarbantia-Carnuntum road geometry per Barrington Atlas 20, Löhberg 2010, Visy 2011, as used in this site's roads_main/roads_secondary layers)

properties.name: Sambia Peninsula
properties.role: The Sambia Peninsula and its adjoining shore were the source zone where the Aesti people gathered raw amber from the shallows and beach, according to Tacitus, lying entirely outside Roman territory as a trading-partner region rather than annexed land.

properties.name: Carnuntum
properties.role: Carnuntum was the Danube crossing and legionary base where the Amber Road entered firmly Roman territory, lying some 600 Roman miles south of the Baltic amber coast by Pliny's count. This node duplicates the town's full site entry elsewhere on the map; here it marks its role as an Amber Road station.

properties.name: Sopron
properties.role: Scarbantia grew from an early trading post on the Amber Road into Municipium Flavium Scarbantia under the Flavian emperors, standing in Pannonia Superior midway between Savaria and Carnuntum.

properties.name: Szombathely
properties.role: Savaria was founded as Colonia Claudia Savariensium for army veterans under Claudius in 43 CE and grew into the junction where the Amber Road met roads running west into Noricum.

properties.name: Sala
properties.role: Sala was a Pannonian road station between Poetovio and Savaria recorded in the Itinerarium Antonini, identified today with the archaeological site at Zalalövő, Hungary.

properties.name: Ptuj
properties.role: Poetovio grew from a legionary base into Colonia Ulpia Traiana Poetovio under Trajan and served as headquarters of the portorium Illyrici, the customs office that taxed goods, including amber, moving along the Danube frontier.

properties.name: Celje
properties.role: Celeia became Municipium Claudium Celeia under Claudius, one of the first towns in Noricum to gain that status, and stood on the Amber Road between Emona and Poetovio.

properties.name: Ljubljana
properties.role: Emona was founded as a Roman colony under Augustus at the head of the Ljubljanica valley, the first major town the Amber Road reached after crossing the Julian Alps from Aquileia.

properties.name: Aquileia
properties.role: Aquileia was the Amber Road's southern terminus and the empire's chief Adriatic gateway for northern trade, home to workshops that carved raw Baltic amber into finished ornaments. This node duplicates the town's full site entry elsewhere on the map; here it marks its role as the Amber Road's terminus.

properties.name: Alexandria-Rome grain route
properties.notes: Egypt was Rome's biggest single grain source - Josephus says it fed the city for four months of the year. The Alexandria run took 10-20 days depending on wind, and the fleet's arrival at Puteoli was a public spectacle: Seneca describes crowds straining to spot the lead ships by their distinctive sail rig. The largest Alexandrian grain carriers, ships like the Isis that Lucian describes at Piraeus, ran some 55 meters long with a cargo capacity near 1,200 tons. By 117 CE most of that traffic had shifted to Trajan's new hexagonal basin at Portus, finished just a few years earlier, though Puteoli kept handling part of the fleet.
sources: Lucian, The Ship, or The Wishes
Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980)

properties.name: Africa-Rome grain route
properties.notes: Africa Proconsularis rivaled Egypt as Rome's grain basket, drawing on the rain-fed wheat estates of the Bagradas valley behind Carthage. Josephus credits Africa with feeding Rome for eight months of the year against Egypt's four - a figure modern historians treat as rounded rather than exact, but it captures how the two provinces together carried most of the city's supply. The crossing to Ostia was shorter and less wind-dependent than the Alexandria run, making African grain a steadier year-round supplement to Egypt's seasonal fleet.
sources: Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980)

properties.name: Sicily-Rome grain route
properties.notes: Sicily was Rome's oldest grain province, worked under a tithe system (the decuma) that Cicero's prosecution of the governor Gaius Verres in 70 BCE exposed as riddled with extortion. By Trajan's day Egypt and Africa had eclipsed it in scale, but Sicily's short, low-risk crossing kept it feeding Rome as a standing supplement rather than the crisis-year backup it's sometimes assumed to have become.

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.role: Alexandria was Rome's single biggest grain terminal, its harbor loading the great Egyptian fleet each sailing season. This node duplicates the city's own gazetteer entry elsewhere on the map; here it marks its role as the grain route's Egyptian terminus.

properties.name: Carthage
properties.role: Carthage shipped the wheat of the Bagradas valley's estates to Rome, making Africa Proconsularis the empire's other great grain province alongside Egypt. This node duplicates the city's own gazetteer entry elsewhere on the map; here it marks its role as the grain route's African terminus.

properties.name: Syracuse
properties.role: Syracuse was one of Sicily's chief grain-tithe collection ports under the Republican decuma system, the oldest link in Rome's grain supply.

properties.name: Marsala
properties.role: Lilybaeum, at Sicily's western tip, was one of the island's main tithe-collection assize centers and a short crossing from Africa and Puteoli alike.

properties.name: Pozzuoli
properties.role: Puteoli was Rome's main grain terminal before Trajan's Portus basin took over most of the traffic; Seneca describes crowds at its harbor spotting the incoming Alexandrian fleet by its sail rig. This node duplicates the town's own site entry elsewhere on the map; here it marks its role on the grain route.

properties.name: Ostia
properties.role: Ostia was Rome's river-mouth port and grain-storage hub at the Tiber's silted mouth, ringed with horrea warehouses that held the city's incoming supply before barges carried it upriver. This node duplicates the town's own site entry elsewhere on the map; here it marks its role on the grain route.
sources: Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980)

properties.name: Portus
properties.role: Trajan's new hexagonal inner basin at Portus, finished only a few years before this map's 117 CE snapshot, had already taken over most of the grain fleet's big-ship traffic from Ostia's silted river channel. This node duplicates the town's own site entry elsewhere on the map; here it marks its role on the grain route.

properties.name: Cornwall-Rome tin route
properties.direction: Ictis (Cornwall) -> Armorica -> mouth of the Rhone -> Massilia -> Rome
properties.notes: Diodorus Siculus, drawing on the eyewitness account of the traveler Posidonius, describes merchants buying tin from the Britons of Cornwall and ferrying it across a tidal strait to the island of Ictis, then carrying it on foot through Gaul for about thirty days before loading it onto pack-horses for the final stretch to the mouth of the Rhone. That overland corridor, not the longer sea route around Iberia past Gades, was the dominant path for British tin reaching Rome by Trajan's day: Strabo says the Massiliotes found the land route through Gaul cheaper and easier than shipping by sea, and a century and a half of Roman peace in Gaul after Caesar's conquest had only made that road safer to use. From the Rhone's mouth the tin moved on by river and coastal boat to Massilia, then by sea to Italy, arriving as ingots that Roman smiths alloyed into bronze fittings, pewter tableware, and coinage alloys sold across the city.

properties.name: St Michael's Mount
properties.role: St Michael's Mount is the most widely accepted candidate for Diodorus's Ictis, a tidal island Britons could reach on foot at low tide to load ingots of Cornish tin onto merchants' carts. Cornwall's tin streams, worked since the Bronze Age, made this stretch of coast the main source of tin the classical Mediterranean world knew. The identification is debated, but the site's tidal causeway matches Diodorus's description more closely than rival candidates like the Isle of Wight or Mount Batten.

properties.name: Vannes
properties.role: Darioritum was the chief town of the Veneti, the Armorican seafaring people Caesar found controlling the Channel trade with Britain and had to crush in a major naval battle in 56 BCE before Rome could bring the tin route under its own control. After the conquest, Armorica's harbors remained the natural landing point for tin ferried across from Cornwall before the thirty-day overland leg into Gaul began.

properties.name: Arles
properties.role: Arelate sat at the point where the tin road's overland leg through Gaul reached the Rhone, the destination Diodorus names for the merchants' thirty-day trek on foot. From here the route shifted from pack-horse to river and coastal shipping for the run down toward Massilia. This node duplicates the town's role on other trade corridors elsewhere on the map; here it marks its place as the tin road's Rhone-mouth transfer point.

properties.name: Marseille
properties.role: Massilia was the Greek-founded port where Gaulish tin entered full Mediterranean shipping lanes, its merchants controlling much of the overland trade Strabo describes moving down from Britain through Gaul. The city's trade ties with the Gallic interior, built up since its founding around 600 BCE, made it the natural clearinghouse before tin ingots sailed on for Italy.

properties.name: Rome
properties.role: Rome was the tin road's final market, where smiths alloyed Cornish tin with copper into bronze and with lead into pewter for tableware, fittings, and coinage alloys sold across the capital. Tin itself left no monumental trace the way grain or oil did, but its presence in nearly every bronze object in the city makes this one of the least visible yet most essential trade routes on this map.

properties.name: Baetica-Rome olive oil route
properties.notes: Baetica's oil growers along the Guadalquivir shipped more olive oil to Rome than any other province in the empire, packed into globular Dressel 20 jars painted with the producer's name, the shipper, the tare weight, and the consular date of loading. Pliny rated Baetican oil among the best in the Mediterranean, and by Trajan's reign the trade had grown large enough that Rome dedicated an entire hill, Monte Testaccio, to the empty jars: an estimated 53 million broken amphorae, more than 80 percent of them from Baetica, eventually built a mound over 35 meters tall. Strabo describes seagoing merchant ships sailing straight up the Guadalquivir to load at Hispalis itself rather than trans-shipping at the coast, cutting out a costly extra handling stage. From there ships ran the Straits of Gibraltar and crossed open water to Ostia and Portus, then continued upriver by barge to unload at Rome's own Tiber-side wharves.
sources: Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980)

properties.name: Cordoba
properties.role: Corduba anchored the upper Guadalquivir stretch of Baetica's olive belt, a valley so densely planted with groves that its oil, alongside grain and wine, made the province one of the wealthiest in the empire. Barges carried its estates' Dressel 20 jars downriver to Hispalis for onward shipment to Rome. This node duplicates the town's role in the region's craft economy documented elsewhere on the map; here it marks its place as an olive oil route origin point.
sources: Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980)

properties.name: Seville
properties.role: Hispalis was Baetica's main river port and the point where the Guadalquivir's oil traffic met open-water shipping; Strabo says seagoing merchant vessels sailed all the way upriver to load here rather than trans-shipping at the coast. Its wharves handled the bulk of the province's Dressel 20 amphora traffic bound for Rome, making it the single busiest node in the empire's olive oil supply chain.

properties.name: Ostia
properties.role: Ostia received Baetican oil ships alongside Rome's grain fleet, its horrea warehouses handling amphorae before Trajan's newer Portus basin took over the largest cargo runs. This node duplicates the town's role on the map's grain routes; here it marks its place in the olive oil supply chain specifically.
sources: Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980)

properties.name: Portus
properties.role: Trajan's new hexagonal basin at Portus, finished only a few years before 117 CE, gave Baetican oil ships a purpose-built harbor to unload into barges bound upriver for Rome. This node duplicates the harbor's role on the map's grain routes; here it marks its place in the olive oil supply chain specifically.

properties.name: Monte Testaccio
properties.role: Monte Testaccio was Rome's dump for the empty Dressel 20 jars that arrived full of Baetican oil, stacked and broken in an orderly enough fashion that archaeologists can still read the tituli picti painted on the sherds: the producer's name, the oil's weight, the shipper, and the exact consular year each jar was loaded. By the time dumping finally stopped in the 3rd century, the mound held an estimated 53 million amphorae and stood more than 35 meters tall, over 80 percent of it Baetican in origin. In 117 CE the hill was already a recognizable landmark next to Rome's river port south of the Aventine, having grown for roughly a century by then.

properties.name: Africa-Rome olive oil route
properties.notes: Africa Proconsularis was already growing into a major olive oil exporter by 117 CE, with groves spreading across Byzacena and Tripolitania on centuriated grids much like Baetica's. Leptis Magna and Hadrumetum shipped oil packed in African cylindrical amphorae, a distinct shape from Baetica's globular Dressel 20 jars, on a shorter and more predictable Mediterranean crossing than the run from Spain. The African trade was still smaller than Baetica's under Trajan - it would not rival and then surpass Spanish oil until the following two centuries - but its groves were expanding fast enough that Baetica's own producers had reason to watch African competition rising across the sea.

properties.name: Leptis Magna
properties.role: Leptis Magna anchored Tripolitania's growing olive oil trade, its hinterland planted with groves on a centuriated grid that Roman surveyors laid out through the pre-desert zone. The city's harbor shipped oil north on the short Mediterranean crossing to Rome, a trade that expanded enormously in the century after Trajan's death. This node duplicates the city's own gazetteer entry elsewhere on the map; here it marks its role as an olive oil route origin point.

properties.name: Sousse
properties.role: Hadrumetum served Byzacena's olive groves as their main Mediterranean outlet, a Phoenician-founded harbor city that predated Carthage itself and kept trading on through the Roman period. Its oil moved north in African cylindrical amphorae, a regional jar type distinct from the Dressel 20 shape Baetica used.

properties.name: Portus
properties.role: Portus received African oil shipments alongside the larger Baetican and Egyptian grain fleets, its Trajanic hexagonal basin only a few years old in 117 CE. This node duplicates the harbor's role on the map's other trade routes; here it marks its place in the African olive oil trade specifically.

properties.name: Silk Road
properties.direction: China to Rome, via Kushan and Parthian territory
properties.notes: Chinese silk crossed Central Asia through Kushan territory and then Parthian Persia, whose rulers ran the middle stretch as a deliberate monopoly, taxing and re-selling raw silk to Roman buyers while keeping its source a closely guarded secret. Caravans reached Palmyra's markets before the final leg to Antioch, Rome's own gateway to eastern luxury goods. A parallel sea route through the Red Sea to Muziris on India's coast fed Alexandria with additional silk, spices, and gems.
sources: The 4 Powerful Empires of the Silk Road, TheCollector

properties.name: Incense Road
properties.direction: Arabia Felix to Gaza and Alexandria
properties.notes: Camel caravans carried frankincense and myrrh some 1,600 miles from the harvest fields of Hadhramaut, watering and paying toll at oasis stations the whole way north. Petra, the Nabataean capital, taxed and redistributed the cargo before it reached Mediterranean shipping at Gaza and Alexandria — and by 117 CE Petra itself sat inside the Roman province of Arabia, folding the old smuggling route directly into imperial revenue.
sources: Madain Project, Cities, Trade Points, and Nodes of the Incense Trade Route

properties.name: Antioch
properties.role: Antioch was the Silk Road's Roman terminus, where caravan goods off-loaded from Palmyra entered the empire's own Mediterranean shipping network.

properties.name: Palmyra
properties.role: Palmyra grew rich as the last great caravan market before the Roman frontier, taxing Silk Road goods as they crossed from Parthian territory into the empire.

properties.name: Dura-Europos
properties.role: This fortified Euphrates river town sat on the contested edge between Roman Syria and Parthia, changing hands repeatedly as a garrison and customs post on the eastern caravan route.

properties.name: Ctesiphon
properties.role: The Parthian capital on the Tigris controlled the silk trade's middle stretch, taxing and re-selling Chinese goods to Roman buyers without ever letting them deal directly with the source.

properties.name: Ecbatana
properties.role: An old Median capital turned Parthian summer residence, Ecbatana anchored the caravan road as it climbed onto the Iranian plateau east of Mesopotamia.

properties.name: Merv
properties.role: Merv was a major oasis city where the Silk Road's Parthian and Kushan-controlled stretches met, a resupply point for caravans crossing Central Asia's deserts.

properties.name: Bactra
properties.role: Bactra, in the Kushan Empire's heartland, was a crossroads city where Chinese, Indian, and Persian trade networks all converged before goods moved on toward Parthia and Rome.

properties.name: Shabwa
properties.role: Shabwa was the capital of the Hadhramaut kingdom and the collection point where frankincense harvested from the surrounding hills was weighed, taxed, and loaded onto northbound caravans.

properties.name: Najran
properties.role: Najran was a major watering stop where the incense caravan route crossed a key north-south trade axis in the Arabian interior.

properties.name: Dedan
properties.role: Dedan was a long-established oasis kingdom in the Hejaz, its wells and markets a fixed stop for caravans on the incense route long before Rome ever taxed the trade.

properties.name: Hegra
properties.role: Hegra was the Nabataeans' second city after Petra, its rock-cut tombs marking the wealth the incense trade brought even to a stop deep in the desert.

properties.name: Petra
properties.role: Petra was the Nabataean capital that built its fortune taxing and redistributing incense caravans, a role it kept after Rome annexed the kingdom as the province of Arabia in 106.

properties.name: Gaza
properties.role: Gaza was the Mediterranean port where incense caravans finally met Roman shipping, the end of a journey that began some 1,600 miles south in Arabia Felix.
